note: City documents published after the workbook, and the sources that ballot.json cites beyond it. Sources here continue the workbook's numbering (S20 onwards). Every quote, here and in ballot.json, must appear on its page of source/excerpts/{source}.json (whitespace-normalized; page 1 for a web page). The build parses every number from its quote, so a number can't drift from its source. News excerpts keep only the paragraphs quoted.

initial-estimate.text: The City's first estimate of the General Fund shortfall, after rebuilding its baseline from actual spending and service needs.

cites.quote: Baseline rebuilt using actual spending and service needs.

revenue-projections.text: Updated revenue projections: the City now expects to collect more than the first estimate assumed, so the gap shrinks.

center-street-debt-service.text: Debt payments for 1947 Center Street that the General Fund has to cover. The City calls it required debt-service support.

parking-funds-stabilization.text: General Fund money to stabilize the City's parking funds.

non-departmental.text: Changes to General Fund costs that don't belong to any one department. The City calls them non-departmental refinements.

adjustments.text: Three changes that add to the gap: debt payments for 1947 Center Street, money to stabilize the parking funds, and costs that don't belong to any one department.

cites.quote: Includes strategic cost shifts, non-departmental refinements, required debt-service support, and parking-fund stabilization.

before-one-time-resources.text: The gap after every revenue and spending adjustment, before any one-time money is used.

cites.quote: After revenue and expenditure adjustments, GF deficit ranged from $31.3M (FY 27) to $29.5M (FY 28)

one-time-resources.text: Money the City can spend only once, used here to even out the FY27 and FY28 gaps. The City says it eases the gap in the short term, and the lasting fix comes from ongoing cuts and new revenue.

cites.quote: Smooth Out Difference in FY 2027 and FY 2028 Deficit
While one-time resources provide short-term easing, the underlying balance is achieved through durable, sustainable fiscal measures and new revenue.

final-gap.text: The gap left after every step: the number the City planned around. The City says it closed it with ongoing cuts of more than 10% of department budgets. It says the underlying balance comes from lasting measures and new revenue.

cites.quote: The City closed the FY 27 and FY 28 structural deficits with more than 10 percent in ongoing reductions.
the underlying balance is achieved through durable, sustainable fiscal measures and new revenue.

costDrivers.text: Why? The City points to rising personnel, pension and health-care costs, inflation, and programs that were paid for with one-time money, along with limits on state and federal revenue.

cites.quote: Rising costs in personnel, pension, and health care • Inflation • Programs supported by one - time funds • State/federal revenue limitations and economic uncertainty

payAndBenefits.text: This year's budget also builds in pay increases already set in labor agreements and higher health, dental and CalPERS pension contributions.

cites.quote: Personnel budgets incorporate projected equity and cost ‑ of ‑ living adjustments pursuant to current labor agreements and updated benefit rates, including health and dental cost increases, CalPERS contribution amounts

auditorRevenues.text: The City Auditor's report on FY 2012 to FY 2021 found that the City's revenues increased and outpaced expenses in most years. It looked at all governmental activities, not just the General Fund.

cites.quote: The City’s revenues have increased since FY 2012 and outpaced expenses most years
We used various financial indicators to analyze the City’s financial condition between FY 2012 and FY 2021
The City’s governmental activities revenues generally outpaced expenses
